title: S3 Fallback
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A default bucket for instances that have no S3 of their own. You name your S3-compatible backends once, then mount each kind of file on one: record uploads, backup zips, PITR history, or any extension's own kind. Every instance gets its own folder in the bucket and can't reach anything outside it. The credentials never reach the instance. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Install
text: S3 Fallback isn't built into pocketone ; add it to a Go build. Under Pocker, add it to the server's extensions: srv := &pocker.Server{Config: cfg, Extensions: []pocker.Extension{s3fallback.New(s3fallback.Config{})}} On a single app, register it with the backends and mounts in Go: extkit.MustRegister(app, s3fallback.New(s3fallback.Config{Backends: backends, Mounts: mounts})) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3-fallback .

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Configure
text: Under Pocker the storage section of pocketone.yaml is read at start. Fields set in Go win. storage: backends: # named S3-compatible destinations r2-eu: { endpoint: https:// .eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, bucket: pocketbase-eu, region: auto, access_key: $R2_KEY, secret: $R2_SECRET } b2-cold: { endpoint: ..., bucket: ph-backups, region: ..., access_key: ..., secret: ... } mounts: # filesystem kind - backend storage: r2-eu # record uploads backups: b2-cold # backup zips litestream: r2-eu # PITR history (ext/pitr) # enabled: false # off for every instance Each backend also takes prefix (prepended to every key, so several deployments can share a bucket) and force_path_style (for MinIO and similar servers). With no mounts the extension does nothing and files stay on local disk, as in PocketBase. Each instance can turn it off in its own settings, from instances.yaml or a mothership. Only enabled is read per instance; backends and mounts are the operator's: instances: id: blog extensions: { storage: { enabled: false } } The old shape ( bucket: with uploads: / backups: ) still works, with a warning: it becomes a backend named default , mounted for uploads and backups.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to do day to day. To an instance nothing is configured: Settings show S3 off, and uploads, thumbs, $app.newFilesystem() and the Backups screen work as before. Files land in the bucket under instances/ / / . Downloads stream through the server, or redirect to the bucket with S3 Redirect. When an instance turns on its own S3 (Settings → Files storage, or Settings → Backups), PocketBase's normal code takes over with the instance's credentials. Files already in the default bucket stay there, as PocketBase's own S3 switch doesn't move files either. It applies to instances created with the extension on. Files already on an instance's local disk are not read or moved.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Each instance gets the root instances/ / ; the storage section is read when the server starts. PITR Mount litestream and every instance without its own bucket keeps its history there. An instance's own PITR bucket still wins. S3 Redirect Downloads become signed redirects to the bucket. Nothing to wire: the fenced filesystem signs with its prefix, so S3 Redirect treats it like any S3 mount.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Building on S3 Fallback
text: Your own kind. Any kind an extension asks for through PocketBase's OnFilesystemCreate is served when it's mounted. PITR's litestream works this way. Uploads and backups step aside when the app turned on its own S3; for other kinds, the extension asking checks its own app setting first. Go API. Bind(app, root) serves an app's filesystems from the mounts under root ( "" for a single app, instances/ / under Pocker). FS(root, kind) returns the same fenced filesystem outside a hook; close it when done. Config() returns the effective configuration.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go yet. storage_test.go and mounts_test.go show it on a single app and under Pocker, against MinIO.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: How it works
text: PocketBase asks OnFilesystemCreate before it creates a filesystem. For a mounted kind, the extension answers with the backend, fenced to / . An instance can't list, read, write or delete anything outside it. The fence is a driver that adds the prefix to every key and strips it from listings. Signed download URLs are made with the backend's own credentials.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Status
text: Works and is tested against MinIO; not yet deployed.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: License

title: S3 Redirect
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree File downloads as short-lived signed redirects to your bucket, after PocketBase's own access check. When an app keeps its files in S3 (Settings → Files storage), PocketBase normally downloads each file from the bucket and streams it to the browser. With S3 Redirect, /api/files/... answers 302 with a presigned GET URL instead, and the browser fetches the file straight from the bucket. The app's bandwidth, memory and connections stay free. With Cloudflare R2 the downloads cost no egress either. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Install
text: S3 Redirect is built into pocketone and on by default . It only acts when S3 file storage is on: turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage and downloads redirect. With files on local disk, nothing changes. To stream files through the app as before: pocketone serve --s3Redirect=false In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: import "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect" app := pocketbase.New() s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) app.Start() Then turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Configure
text: Set it in pocketone.yaml : s3redirect: enabled: true # false streams files through the app ttl: 5m # how long each signed URL is valid Or with flags, which win over the file: --s3Redirect true Redirect downloads when S3 file storage is on. --s3Redirect=false streams them. --s3RedirectTTL 5m How long each signed URL stays valid (at most 7 days). Keep the TTL short: anyone holding a URL can fetch the file until it expires, protected files included. The bucket itself is PocketBase's own S3 setting, in Settings → Files storage . There are no other settings screens. Bucket CORS. A redirect followed by fetch() or from your site needs a CORS rule on the bucket allowing GET from your origin. Plain , and links need nothing.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: s3redirect:
text: Signed S3 redirects for file downloads: enabled, URL lifetime. The --s3Redirect and --s3RedirectTTL flags win. enabled bool On unless false (it only acts when S3 file storage is on). Flag: --s3Redirect. ttl duration How long each signed URL stays valid. Default 5m, max 7 days. Flag: --s3RedirectTTL.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Use
text: Once S3 is on, there's nothing to click. File URLs stay the same; they answer with a redirect: Access checks don't change. PocketBase still finds the record, checks protected-file tokens and the view rule, and creates thumbnails on first request. The redirect happens only after all of that. The file token stays private. It never goes into the bucket URL, and the redirect sends Referrer-Policy: no-referrer . Same headers as PocketBase: inline or attachment ( ?download=1 ), the filename, and forced content types (SVG, CSS, JS) are signed into the URL as S3 response- overrides. Range requests work, because S3 serves them. Caching: the browser may reuse the redirect for 80% of the TTL ( Cache-Control: private , never shared caches); the file itself gets PocketBase's usual 30-day Cache-Control . Falls back to streaming when S3 is off, the extension is turned off, or signing fails. A failed signature logs a warning, s3redirect: signing failed, streaming instead . Only GET and HEAD requests are redirected. Inline vs attachment: PocketBase decides this from the stored content type; S3 Redirect goes by the file extension (it doesn't ask the bucket, so a redirect costs no extra round trip). They agree for every file PocketBase names.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Try it
text: cd example && go run . serve The example runs one app with its own in-process bucket, nothing to set up. It: starts an S3-compatible bucket on 127.0.0.1:9199 (gofakes3, objects kept in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt ), and points the app's Files storage at it; seeds a demo_files record with an image (thumbs 100x100 ) and a protected text file, uploaded through PocketBase; prints the URLs to open. Each answers 302 to the bucket. The bucket only serves presigned GETs whose signature, re-computed with the AWS SDK's own SigV4 signer , matches and hasn't expired, and logs each one ( demo bucket: presigned GET ..., signature valid ). Unsigned or edited URLs get 403 . So a working download proves the signatures are AWS-compatible, not just accepted by a lenient fake. S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 skips the demo bucket (use your own Files storage settings); S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR moves it. The example is its own Go module, so its demo dependencies (gofakes3, the AWS SDK signer) never reach the extension's go.mod .

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Works with
text: Pocker The same extension runs on every instance. The s3redirect section sets the defaults; each instance can override enabled and ttl (below). S3 Fallback Apps without their own S3 settings keep files in its bucket (under pocker, fenced to instances/ /storage/ ). Its driver signs, so those downloads redirect too.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: srv.Extensions = append(srv.Extensions, s3redirect.New(s3redirect.Config{})) s3redirect: # server defaults enabled: true # on unless false ttl: 5m instances: id: abc extensions: s3redirect: { enabled: false } # per instance: enabled, ttl It's an extkit extension, so the same value works on a single app and on every pocker instance; it doesn't link pocker.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Building on S3 Redirect
text: Supply your own bucket. S3 Redirect signs for whatever filesystem PocketBase serves the download from: the app's own S3 settings, or one an extension supplies through OnFilesystemCreate . Implement s3redirect.Signer ( SignedURL(key, ttl, now, overrides) ) on your filesystem driver and its downloads redirect. Nothing else needs wiring; a filesystem that can't sign (local disk) streams as usual. Your own download handlers run first. The extension binds OnFileDownloadRequest last (priority 1000, id s3redirect.HookID , __ext_s3redirect__ ), so your Go or JS handlers can still change the served file or answer themselves without calling e.Next() . Unbind the id to turn it off for one app.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Example
text: example/main.go starts its own in-process S3 bucket, points the app's file storage at it and seeds a record, so every download redirect works with nothing to set up. Run go run . serve in example/ and open the URLs it prints. // Command example runs one PocketOne app whose file downloads redirect to an S3 bucket, with nothing to set up: // it starts its own S3-compatible bucket in-process (gofakes3, stored in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt), points the app's // Files storage at it, and seeds a "demo_files" record with an image and a protected document. // // go run . serve // // Open the URLs it prints. Each answers 302 with a signed URL; the bucket logs every fetch and only serves it if the // signature is valid and unexpired, checked independently with the AWS SDK's SigV4 signer. // // Set S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 to skip the demo bucket and use whatever Files storage you configure in the dashboard. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) if os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO") != "0" { addr := os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR") if addr == "" { addr = "127.0.0.1:9199" } registerDemo(app, addr) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Redirect
heading: How it works
text: Go module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect , no dependencies beyond PocketOne. The redirect is an OnFileDownloadRequest handler; the hook already exists upstream, so there's no core change. Signing is SigV4 query-string auth in sigv4 , checked against AWS's documented example. It needs no change to PocketBase's S3 client. The TTL is clamped to between 1 second and 7 days.

title: Sandbox
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Confines one PocketOne app's JS hooks and migrations, so apps from people you don't know can share one process. File access stays inside the app's folder, host primitives are gone, every JS call has a time limit, raw SQL can't leave the app's own database files, and outbound connections reach public addresses only. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Sandbox
heading: Install
text: Sandbox isn't a switch in pocketone : Pocker applies it to every instance it runs. With a multisite section in pocketone.yaml (pocker as the runtime), every instance is sandboxed and there's nothing to install. A single app served by pocketone without a multisite section is not sandboxed. In your own Go build, give it to the JSVM engine as an extension: sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{Dir: dir, Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}} execution, sleep := sb.Limits() jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []any{sb}, VM: jsvm.VMConfig{TaskWall: execution, MaxSleep: sleep}, }) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/sandbox . The SQL guard and the outbound network rules are separate calls (see Integrations).

title: Sandbox
heading: Configure
text: Sandbox has no pocketone.yaml section of its own. Under Pocker its limits are set in the pocker section, as defaults for every instance, and each instance can override them in its own limits : pocker: max_js_execution: 30s # each JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after this max_js_allocation: 64MiB # biggest single file read or reader JS can ask for max_call_stack_size: 2000 # unused: the JS engine caps its stack by size max_sleep: 10s # cap on sleep() max_query_duration: 30s # deadline for SQL statements that have none http_send_max_timeout: 60s # cap on $http.send timeouts http_send_max_body: 10MiB # cap on $http.send response size max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls one instance runs at once egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach, such as an internal SMTP relay The values shown are Pocker's defaults. An instance gets only its own secrets as environment. In a Go build, the same settings are Sandbox fields: Dir (required), Env , MaxExecution (default 30 s, negative turns it off), MaxSleep , MaxAllocation , HTTPSendMaxTimeout , HTTPSendMaxBody , and Console to send console. output somewhere other than the process's stdout and stderr. Limits() gives the execution and sleep limits for jsvm.Config.VM ; the memory cap and MaxConcurrent are set there too.

title: Sandbox
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to operate day to day. Hooks that stick to normal app code ( routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest) run unchanged. What changes for a hook author: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit and $filesystem.local fail with "not available on this host (sandboxed)"; $os.args is empty; process-wide Go methods such as $app.restart read as undefined . Files outside the app's folder can't be read or written, by any API, including through .. or symlinks. $os.getenv and process.env see only the app's own environment. A JS call that runs past its time limit is interrupted with an error; so is one that asks for a huge allocation. $http.send to a private or loopback address is refused. Under Pocker, console. output and hook errors go to the instance's own logs/exec.log .

title: Sandbox
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Runs every instance through the sandbox, the SQL guard and the outbound network rules, with limits from the pocker section and each instance's limits . Its attack tests are in sandbox_test.go . Multisite Carries the per-instance limits from instances.yaml or a mothership. Firewall Rate and concurrency limits in front of every request. Docker The alternative for untrusted apps: a container per instance instead of checks inside one process. Docker doesn't use the sandbox.

title: Sandbox
heading: Building on Sandbox
text: Sandbox is a jsvm extension ( OnInit , Modules , HTTPClient , and HideField / HideMethod to hide process-reaching Go members); add it to jsvm.Config.Extensions . GuardedDBConnect(maxQuery) is a core.DBConnectFunc : set it as the app's DBConnect to open the databases through SQLite's authorizer, with a deadline for statements that have none. InstallEgressPolicy(sandbox.EgressPolicy{Allow: ...}) routes Go's default HTTP transport through the public-only dialer, for the whole process. EgressPolicy.Dialer() gives the same check for your own connections. BindMail(app) sends the app's own SMTP through that dialer. ErrSandboxed is the error disabled bindings return.

title: Sandbox
heading: Example
text: One app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access confined to the app folder, host primitives disabled, and a 5 s limit per JS call. Run it from this folder with go run ./example serve . // Command example runs one PocketOne app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access is confined to the app folder, // host primitives ($os.exec, $os.exit, ...) are disabled, and every JS call has a time limit. // // go run ./example serve // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "path/filepath" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/sandbox" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" dir, _ := os.Getwd() sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{ Dir: dir, // JS may only touch this folder Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}, // the only environment JS sees MaxExecution: 5 time.Second, } jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []any{sb}, // OnInit, Modules, HTTPClient and the member filter }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Sandbox
heading: How is this safe?
text: With pocker, PocketOne can serve hundreds of instances from one Go process, each with its own owner, hooks and data. This section explains why that's safe enough to run code from people you don't know, and where it isn't. Configuration and the engine API are in POCKER.md. The attack tests are in sandbox_test.go .

title: Sandbox
heading: Why one process
text: Most hosted PocketBase instances are idle most of the time. A container per instance means paying idle memory and a cold start of a second or more for each one. In one process an instance's app starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, costs a few MB while it runs, and shares the Go runtime with everyone else. What you give up is the kernel boundary between tenants. Everything below replaces it with checks inside the process.

title: Sandbox
heading: The threat
text: Assume every instance's owner is hostile. They control: their pb_hooks (JavaScript, run by the instance's own QuickJS VM, ext/jsvm); their pb_migrations ; their collections, rules and settings; any SQL their hooks run; requests to their own instance. They must not be able to: read or change another instance's files, database, environment or settings; read the host's files, environment, credentials or private network; take the process down, or starve everyone else of CPU and memory.

title: Sandbox
heading: 1. Each instance is its own app
text: Every instance has its own core.App , database, settings, JS VMs, migrations list, settings encryption key and log. Requests are routed by hostname to exactly one app. Nothing in one app holds a reference to another. In production only hostnames the instance source maps are served; unknown hosts get 404 and never create a folder.

title: Sandbox
heading: 2. Files: confined by the kernel, not by string checks
text: Every file API reachable from JS goes through an os.Root opened on the instance's folder. That covers: $os. $filepath.glob / walk $filesystem.fileFromPath $template.loadFiles $apis.static require() The kernel resolves each path beneath that root and refuses .. and symlinks that lead out. There is no path string for an attacker to get clever with.

title: Sandbox
heading: 3. Host primitives: removed
text: The following are gone from JS: process control: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args ; $filesystem.local ; PocketBase internals that reach the whole process: $app.restart , bootstrap , onServe , onTerminate , raw hook triggers, sql.DB handles; Go's os/exec , net , syscall and database/sql/driver . A field-name mapper hides them, so they read as undefined . Everything a normal app uses still works: routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest.

title: Sandbox
heading: 4. Environment: only the instance's own
text: $os.getenv and process.env return the instance's own secrets and nothing else. Platform values never go through the environment: the settings encryption key; superusers the host keeps in sync; private tokens for the host's Go code.

title: Sandbox
heading: 5. SQL: SQLite's own authorizer
text: Raw SQL is allowed ( $app.db().newQuery(...) ), because PocketBase apps depend on it. Instead of parsing statements, PocketOne installs SQLite's authorizer callback on every connection, so SQLite itself refuses: ATTACH and VACUUM INTO outside the instance's pb_data ; load_extension ; the pragmas that move SQLite's files elsewhere. Statements without a deadline get one ( max_query_duration ).

title: Sandbox
heading: 6. Outbound network: public addresses only
text: PocketOne installs one dialer process-wide, on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client. It covers: $http.send $filesystem.fileFromURL S3 storage and backups OAuth2/JWKS fetches SMTP The dialer refuses: loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata; CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges; the IPv6 forms of all of these, including IPv4-in-IPv6. It checks the address actually connected to, after DNS, so DNS rebinding doesn't help. $http.send timeouts and response sizes are capped.

title: Sandbox
heading: 7. CPU, memory and concurrency
text: CPU Every JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after max_js_execution , Go calls included. sleep() is capped. Concurrency At most max_concurrent_js JS calls per instance in flight at once; more wait, then fail. Per-IP and per-instance rate and concurrency limits sit in front of every request. Memory Each instance's VM has a hard cap (default 64 MiB): the JS heap plus the Go objects JS holds. A script that grows past it, slowly or at once, gets an out-of-memory error; other instances are unaffected. The JS stack is capped by size, so deep recursion is an error, never a crash. File reads are capped at max_js_allocation . Every limit has a process default and a per-instance override.

title: Sandbox
heading: 8. Failures stay with their instance
text: A broken hooks file, a panic during start or a failed migration fails that instance alone: it answers 502 and logs to its own logs/exec.log . Every other instance keeps serving. console. output goes to the instance's own log, never to the host's.

title: Sandbox
heading: What it doesn't cover
text: Be clear about these before you host strangers: Go memory is estimated. Go objects JS holds are charged to the instance by estimate, and Go's garbage collector can let the process use up to about twice that; set GOMEMLIMIT for the process. It's one address space. A bug in Go, QuickJS, SQLite or PocketOne's own checks would cross tenants in a way a container boundary wouldn't. The sandbox tests cover the known paths, but they don't prove nothing else exists. No OS-level layer yet. Seccomp, Landlock and a second, OS-level egress filter aren't built in.

title: Sandbox
heading: How to run it
text: For untrusted tenants, add the OS layers yourself: run PocketOne as a non-root user that owns only the instances folder; run it under a cgroup memory limit (with swap), so the worst case is a restart, not a host OOM; add an OS firewall rule that lets that user reach public addresses only, an egress layer independent of the process; keep secrets for host code out of the process environment; use private: values instead; put a proxy or the built-in firewall in front, with rate limits on. If you only run your own apps, the defaults are already more than stock PocketBase gives you.

text: MIT

title: Server Timing
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree A Server-Timing response header on every request to an instance of a multisite host: how long the instance's own handler took, and how long it took to wake the instance for the request (under Pocker). Your browser's dev tools show it in the request's Timing tab. Server-Timing: origin;dur=12.4, wake;dur=0.0 Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Server Timing
heading: Install
text: Server Timing is built into pocketone and on whenever it serves many instances, whatever the provider. There's nothing to install. It isn't used for a single app. In your own host build, list it first among the host extensions, so its header covers every other hop: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Extensions: []multisite.Extension{servertiming.New() / , other host extensions /}}) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/servertiming .

title: Server Timing
heading: Configure
text: There's nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen.

title: Server Timing
heading: Use
text: Open your browser's dev tools, pick a request to an instance and look at its timing, or read the header with curl: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/health grep -i server-timing origin The instance's own handler: from handing it the request until it sent its response headers. wake Starting the instance for this request. 0 when it was already running. Each value is in milliseconds, one decimal, up to the response headers (time to first byte). The innermost hop comes first; values a server in front already sent are kept, and this host's entries are added after them.

title: Server Timing
heading: Integrations
text: Pocker registers origin and wake for every request it hands to an instance. Add your own entries. Host code and other extensions call multisite.Timing(ctx, fn) during a request; fn returns []multisite.TimingEntry{{Name, Dur, Desc}} and runs when the headers go out. Only extensions listed after Server Timing are covered. Put names in Desc , never addresses. Go API. FormatTiming , AppendServerTiming and WithServerTiming render entries, append them to a header and wrap a response writer, for a server that isn't a multisite host.

title: Server Timing
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go . See it used in examples/pocketone/multi.go , which lists it first in the pocketone binary's host extensions.

title: Server Timing
heading: How it works
text: It's a host wrapper ( multisite.Wrapper ). For each request it starts collecting timing entries in the request's context, then stamps them into the Server-Timing header just before the response headers go out (not on interim 1xx responses). Flush, Hijack and http.ResponseController keep working through its writer.

title: Settings
heading: Install
text: Settings is built into pocketone and on by default ; there's nothing to install. In your own Go build: extkit.Setup(app, []extkit.Extension{settings.New(), pitr.New(pitr.Config{})}, nil, nil) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/settings .

title: Settings

title: Standard Set
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree The extensions every PocketOne app has: settings, API tokens (with the OAuth server), remotes (remote/v1), MCP, PocketPages, S3 redirects, point-in-time restore, backups, bulk mail and deploy. The stock pocketone binary and every Pocker instance use it, so an app never misses one because its host forgot to list it. Members can be reconfigured or turned off per app, never removed. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Standard Set
heading: Install
text: The standard set is built into pocketone . In your own Go build, make the app with it instead of pocketbase.New() : set := standard.New() app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"}) app.Start() NewApp registers the members, loads pb_hooks with their JS APIs ( $mcp , $tokens , $bulkmail ) and resolves their contracts. On an app you built yourself, call set.Register(app, jsvmConfig) instead.

title: Standard Set
heading: Configure
text: Reconfigure a member: replace it, e.g. set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 24 time.Hour}) . A member set to nil is an error. Turn one off: enabled: false in its pocketone.yaml section, or in an instance's extensions. under Pocker. Extensions that require it turn off too, and say why. Add your own: set.Add(myextension.New()) . Extras register after the members, under the same rules. Pick providers: set.Providers is pocketone.yaml 's providers: section, for a contract more than one extension provides.

title: Standard Set
heading: providers:
text: Which extension provides a contract when several do.

title: Standard Set
heading: Use
text: Each app logs what it got when it starts: standard: on: settings, tokens, remotes, mcp, pages, s3redirect, pitr, backups, bulkmail, deploy standard: tokens/v1 ← tokens With remotes off (deploy requires its remote/v1): standard: remotes off: enabled: false standard: deploy off: needs remote/v1, which nothing provides

title: Standard Set
heading: Integrations
text: Pocker Every instance gets the set ( Server.Standard ), with its own extensions. settings. Contracts Members find each other through contracts ( tokens/v1 ), resolved per app; the startup lines show who provides what.

title: Standard Set
heading: Example
text: // A PocketOne app with the standard set and one extra extension: run it with go run . serve . package main import ( "log" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pitr" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/standard" ) func main() { set := standard.New() set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 24 time.Hour}) // reconfigure a member set.Add(mailtrap.New()) // add your own app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Stats
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Looks after the data of the instances a host serves. Today it measures facts about each instance (disk used, last request served) and reports them. Later it will also carry out decisions about that data, such as archiving. Status. Working, first step: facts and the measure decision. Archiving, restoring, offloading backups and purging come next, as further decisions. The rules engine is ready as a Go library but isn't read from pocketone.yaml yet. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Stats
heading: Install
text: Lifecycle runs on a host that serves many instances (ext/multisite, with pocker or docker), not on a single app. The stock pocketone binary turns it on by itself in host mode: when pocketone.yaml has a multisite section, every instance under the first runtime's root folder is measured. There's no switch to flip. multisite: {} instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } In your own host build, add it as a gate (to see requests) and a background job: lc := &stats.Lifecycle{Directory: h.Directory, Folder: func(i multisite.Instance) string { return filepath.Join(root, i.ID) }} h.Gates = append(h.Gates, lc) // records each local instance's last request h.Background = append(h.Background, lc.Run) // measures and reports on the policy's schedule Folder says where an instance's data lives. The stock binary uses the instance's own dir when it has one, else / .

title: Stats
heading: Configure
text: The lifecycle section in pocketone.yaml sets the schedule. Everything is optional. lifecycle: measure_every: 24h # how old a disk measurement may get report_every: 1h # how often changed last-request times are reported concurrency: 2 # instances measured at once

title: Stats
heading: The policy
text: What to do comes from a policy. The built-in one ( YAMLPolicy ) reads this section and decides one thing: measure an instance when it was never measured, or when its measurement is older than measure_every . Zero or missing values fall back to the defaults. Rules with criteria, all / any / not , vetoes and budgets exist in the rules engine, but the lifecycle section doesn't take them yet.

title: Stats
heading: lifecycle:
text: Instance data on this host: how often disk use is measured and last-request times are reported. measure_every duration 24h0m0s How old an instance's disk measurement may get before it is measured again. Default 24h. report_every duration 1h0m0s How often changed last-request times are reported to the sink. Default 1h. concurrency int 2 How many instances are measured at once. Default 2.

title: Stats
heading: What it measures
text: For each instance this host serves itself (not the ones it forwards to another edge): disk_bytes : the size of the regular files in the instance's folder (symlinks aren't followed; 0 when there's no folder), and measured_at , when that was measured. last_active : the last request this host served for it, recorded at most once a minute per instance.

title: Stats
heading: When
text: As soon as the instance list loads, every instance is measured, because none has been measured yet. After that it checks once a minute and measures the instances whose measurement is older than measure_every . Changed last-request times are reported every report_every . Facts are kept in memory. With the default log sink, a restart measures everything again.

title: Stats
heading: What you'll see
text: Log lines from the default sink and the measuring pass: INFO lifecycle: facts instances=12 disk_bytes=48213504 INFO lifecycle: measured instances=12 disk_bytes=48213504 ms=37 lifecycle: facts is each report the sink receives (after a measuring pass, and for last-request times). lifecycle: measured follows a measuring pass, with how long it took. Problems show as warnings: lifecycle: measuring (a folder couldn't be read), lifecycle: report (the sink failed; last-request times are retried next time) and lifecycle: policy .

title: Stats
heading: Try it
text: example/main.go measures the instance folders under a root once and prints each instance's size: go run ./example --root ./pb_root --instances instances.yaml

title: Stats
heading: Works with
text: Multisite Lifecycle is a multisite.Gate (it sees each request to record last_active ) and a host background job ( Run ). It lists instances from multisite.Directory . Pocker Instances under pocker.root (default ./pb_root ), one folder per instance. Docker Instances under docker.root , the same / layout. It knows nothing about plans, payments or tenants: that belongs to whichever policy provider is configured.

title: Stats
heading: Your own policy
text: Set Lifecycle.Policy to anything that implements PolicyProvider : type PolicyProvider interface { Decide(ctx context.Context, facts []Facts) ([]Decision, error) // what to do now, and why ReportEvery() time.Duration // how often last-request times are reported Concurrency() int // instances worked on at once } A control plane can provide its own, for example one that delegates the decisions to a mothership, and providers can wrap each other. Only the measure action is carried out today; any other action is logged as lifecycle: action not supported yet .

title: Stats
heading: Your own sink
text: Set Lifecycle.Sink to anything that implements Sink ( Report(ctx, facts []Facts) error ) to send facts somewhere other than the log. A sink that also implements Loader ( Load(ctx) ([]Facts, error) ) gives the facts back at start, so a restart doesn't measure everything again or forget last-request times.

title: Stats
heading: Rules: criteria an app can replace
text: rules (package github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/stats/rules , standard library only) is the engine policies are built from, on an edge or a mothership. A subject is whatever the caller evaluates: an instance's facts on an edge, an account with its instances on a mothership. Criteria answer one question about a subject (stale? orphaned? over its plan?) and say why. They live in a Registry by name: an app registers its own or replaces a built-in one ( Register("stale", ...) ), and every rule that refers to the name ( Ref("stale") ) follows, so what "stale" means is the app's to decide. Where they come from is pluggable too: code, or definitions from config ( Load ) built from kinds the app registered ( RegisterKind("idle", ...) ) and combined with all , any and not . A YAML section and a mothership are both just sources of definitions. Load registers nothing when a definition is wrong. Rules lead from a criterion to an action, with named vetoes that always win and a budget per run. Reports list each decision with its reasons, what was vetoed and by what, what the budget held back and what failed. Summary gives one line per rule ( archive-stale: 3 decided, 1 vetoed ). Evaluating does nothing by itself: acting on the decisions, or only logging them in a dry run, is the caller's. A definition, as config would supply it: stale: { kind: idle, params: { after: 8760h } } archivable: { kind: all, of: [stale, free_plan] } keep: { kind: not, of: [archivable] } And in Go: r := rules.NewRegistryFacts r.RegisterKind("idle", idleFor) // params: { after: 8760h } _ = r.Load(map[string]rules.Def{ "stale": {Kind: "idle", Params: map[string]any{"after": "8760h"}}, "archivable": {Kind: "all", Of: []string{"stale", "free_plan"}}, }) e := rules.Engine[Facts]{Key: id, Rules: []rules.Rule[Facts]{{ Name: "archive-stale", Action: "archive", When: r.Ref("archivable"), Unless: []rules.Veto[Facts]{{Name: "pinned", If: r.Ref("pinned")}}, Budget: 200, }}} report := e.Evaluate(ctx, facts) Every rule sees every subject, so one subject can get several decisions. Make rules exclusive by building them from exclusive criteria.

title: Stats
heading: Example
text: example/main.go measures the instance folders under a root once and prints their facts, which is what a host's lifecycle does daily. // Measure the instance folders under a root once and print their facts (what a host's lifecycle does daily). // // go run ./example --root ./pb_root --instances instances.yaml package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "log" "log/slog" "path/filepath" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/multisite" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/stats" ) func main() { root := flag.String("root", "./pb_root", "one folder per instance: / ") instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file") flag.Parse() src := &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: instances, Required: true} list, err := src.Snapshot(context.Background()) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } dir := multisite.NewDirectory(slog.Default()) dir.Load(list) lc := &stats.Lifecycle{ Directory: dir, Folder: func(i multisite.Instance) string { if i.Dir != "" { return i.Dir } return filepath.Join( root, i.ID) }, Sink: stats.LogSink{}, } lc.Step(context.Background()) // never measured: every instance is measured now for _, f := range lc.Local() { fmt.Printf("%-24s %12d bytes\n", f.Instance, f.DiskBytes) } }

title: Stats
heading: How it works
text: Go module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/stats . The stock binary wires it in examples/pocketone/multi.go . Run loads recorded facts from a Loader sink, then waits for the host's instance list to load (checking every second). From then on, once a minute, it asks the policy for decisions on the current facts, measures the instances it was asked to ( concurrency at a time) and reports what it measured to the sink. Measuring walks the folder and adds up regular file sizes. An instance's pending last-request time goes out with its measurement, so it isn't reported twice. Admit records last_active only for instances this host serves itself ( Remote empty), and never refuses a request.

title: Tokens
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree Long-lived API tokens for your app: secrets that start with pbt_ , for CI, deploys, scripts and agents. Each token belongs to an account and acts as that account. It can be limited to scopes, given an expiry, and revoked on its own. Send one as Authorization: Bearer pbt_… . Ordinary PocketBase auth tokens keep working unchanged. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Tokens
heading: Install
text: Tokens is built into pocketone and always on. There's nothing to install or turn on. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) app.Start() To use $tokens in pb_hooks , bind it in jsvm's OnInit (the stock binary does): jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { tokens.BindJS(app, rt) }}) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens .

title: Tokens
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or environment variable for Tokens. In pocketone : any account (a superuser, or a record of any auth collection) can own tokens; a token never expires unless you give it an expiry. A Go build can narrow both (see Go config).

title: Tokens
heading: Scopes
text: A token without scopes has its owner's full rights. A token with scopes works only on the requests its scopes cover, plus remote/v1's whoami ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ); anywhere else it gets 403 . Extensions and your own pb_hooks register the scopes. In pocketone the built-in ones are: deploy Deploy Deploy code (hooks, migrations, public files, packages), read files and logs superusers deploy:read Deploy Read deployed files and stream logs superusers pocketone token scopes lists every scope your app has, with its paths.

title: Tokens
heading: Your own scopes
text: Declare a scope at the top level of a pb_hooks file. It then shows up in Settings → API tokens and on the the OAuth server consent page: // pb_hooks/scopes.pb.js $tokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:read', // lower-case letters, digits, ":" and "_" description: 'Read notes', // shown in the token screen and on the consent page paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'], // URL prefixes where a token holding it works methods: ['GET'], // optional: only these methods (GET covers HEAD) }) $tokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:write', description: 'Change notes', paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'] }) collections: ['users'] limits which accounts may hold the scope. Registering a name again merges its paths, methods and collections, so reloading hooks is safe. Two names whose headers would be the same ( notes:write and notes_write ) can't both be registered. Check a scope on your own route: routerAdd('POST', '/api/notes/archive', (e) = { / ... / }, $apis.requireAuth(), $tokens.requireScope('notes:write')) $tokens.requireScope refuses a signed-out request, and a token that doesn't hold the scope. Inside a handler, $tokens.hasScope(e, 'notes:write') tells you the same. Check a scope in a collection API rule. Every signed-in request carries X-Token-Scope- : 1 for each scope it holds, and rules read it as @request.headers.x_token_scope_ ( : becomes _ ): @request.auth.id = owner && @request.headers.x_token_scope_notes_write = "1" A PocketBase auth token or an unscoped API token holds every registered scope (except ones its collection can't hold). A scoped token holds only its own scopes. A signed-out request holds none. Headers a client sends with that prefix are always dropped, so they can't be forged. $tokens.ruleField('notes:write') returns the rule field for a name, and $tokens.scopes() lists every registered scope with its header and rule field.

title: Tokens
heading: From the dashboard
text: Open Settings → API tokens (under Access ). Only superusers see this screen. Fill in a Name . Optionally set Expires in (days) , and tick any Scopes (none means full rights). By default the token is yours. To make one for another account, fill in Owner collection (default _superusers ) and Owner (id or email) . Click Create token . Copy the token now: it's shown only once and never stored. The list shows each token's name, its first characters, owner, scopes, expiry and when it was last used (time and IP). Tokens issued by the OAuth server carry an oauth: label. Click Revoke and confirm to delete one; anything using it stops working at once. App users who aren't superusers manage their own tokens through the REST API.

title: Tokens
heading: From the command line
text: The token command works on the local data dir, like superuser , so you can set up tokens before the first serve: pocketone token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci --scope deploy --ttl 720h # prints the secret pocketone token create --collection users --record user@example.com --name script pocketone token list # every token, or one owner's with an owner flag pocketone token revoke [ ...] pocketone token revoke --all --superuser admin@example.com pocketone token scopes Pick the owner with --superuser , or --collection --record . --scope can be repeated; without --ttl the token never expires.

title: Tokens
heading: Using a token
text: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_…" https://myapp.example.com/api/collections/notes/records An invalid, revoked or expired token leaves the request signed out, like an invalid PocketBase token. A scoped token used outside its scopes gets 403 ("This API token's scopes (…) don't allow this request."). A token can't be exchanged for a PocketBase auth token ( auth-refresh and impersonate refuse it), so revoking a token really ends its access. Expired tokens are deleted once a day. Deleting an account deletes its tokens.

title: Tokens
heading: In the logs
text: A rejected token is logged at debug level: tokens: rejected API token . The daily cleanup logs tokens: deleted expired tokens with a count when it deletes any, and tokens: delete expired as a warning if it fails.

title: Tokens
heading: Works with
text: OAuth (in Tokens) Its access tokens are API tokens, issued with the client's id, the granted scopes and, when asked for, an audience. They show up under Settings → API tokens and can be revoked there. The OAuth server needs Tokens on the app. MCP An agent's OAuth sign-in to /mcp is an API token bound to /mcp that never expires; revoke it to disconnect the agent. Tool calls run as the token's owner. A full-access token's calls hold every registered scope; a token limited to scopes on the consent page has its calls checked like requests with those scopes ( WithScopes ). Deploy Registers deploy and deploy:read ; a deploy token is what CI uses. Remotes pocketone login takes a pasted API token when the remote has no OAuth server. In CI, put a token in P1_TOKEN (or P1_TOKEN_ ). remote/v1's whoami ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ) reports a token's id and scopes, whatever its scopes. Pocker Add tokens.New(tokens.Config{}) to the host's extensions and every instance gets its own tokens, routes and screen. Per instance, extensions: {tokens: {enabled: false}} turns it off and collections: [...] picks who may own tokens. The stock pocketone binary doesn't add it to pocker instances.

title: Tokens
heading: Building on Tokens
text: Register a scope from Go. Extensions register their scopes on the app, usually on bootstrap, and guard their routes: tk := tokens.For(app) tk.MustRegisterScope(tokens.Scope{ Name: "notes:write", Description: "Change notes", Paths: []string{"/api/collections/notes/records"}, Methods: []string{"POST", "PATCH", "DELETE"}, // optional Collections: []string{"users"}, // optional: who may hold it }) se.Router.POST("/api/notes/archive", h).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), tokens.RequireScope("notes:write")) Guards. A Go scope can add Match func( core.RequestEvent) bool : a token with the scope also works on any request it returns true for. It runs before the owner is loaded, so it may look only at the request. Shared scopes. Registering a name again merges its paths, methods, guards and collections, so several extensions can share one scope. Read the token on a request. tokens.FromRequest(e) returns the token a request used (nil for a PocketBase auth token), with its Owner , Scopes and Audience . tokens.HasScope(e, "x") is true for PocketBase auth tokens and unscoped API tokens. Without importing this package. Other extensions use the tokens/v1 contract instead: tokensv1.Contract.Of(app) registers scopes ( RegisterScope ), lists them and checks Reaches ; tokensv1.FromRequest(e) is the request's token (its Grant : owner, scopes, audience, client id); tokensv1.WithScopes limits in-process requests. Deploy and MCP work this way. The X-Token-Scope- headers work for rules and JS. Audience. A token created with CreateOptions.Audience (the OAuth server sets it from the RFC 8707 resource parameter) only works under that URL's path, plus remote/v1's whoami ( /api/_c/remote/v1 ); elsewhere it gets 403 . When the audience has a path (like https://host/mcp ), the token works there whatever its scopes: the scopes limit what that endpoint does on the token's behalf (MCP passes them on with WithScopes ), not the endpoint itself. Limit in-process requests. tokens.WithScopes(ctx, scopes) returns a context whose requests are checked like a token limited to scopes , whatever credential they carry: 403 where the scopes don't reach, and only those scopes in the X-Token-Scope- headers and HasScope . Requests made inside them with the same context inherit the limit, and a nested WithScopes only narrows it. No client value can set it. tokens.ScopesFromContext(ctx) reads it. Reaches(scopes, method, pattern) says whether scopes could cover a route pattern ( {name} segments match anything), and Scope.Infrastructure() whether a scope only reaches contract APIs ( /api/_c/ ). Go API. tokens.For(app) returns the service: Create(owner, CreateOptions{Name, Scopes, Expires, ClientId, Audience}) returns the secret and record; also Verify(secret) , List(owner) , Get(id) , Revoke(id) , RevokeAll(owner) , DeleteExpired() , RegisterScope , MustRegisterScope , Scopes() , Collections() and AllowedCollection(c) . tokens.BindJS(vm, app) adds $tokens ; the extkit extension ( tokens.New ) also binds it. JS. $tokens.registerScope({name, description, paths, methods, collections}) , $tokens.requireScope(name) , $tokens.hasScope(e, name) , $tokens.ruleField(name) and $tokens.scopes() .

title: Tokens
heading: REST API (tokens/v1)
text: The tokens/v1 contract, at /api/_c/tokens/v1 . Any signed-in account; superusers see and manage everyone's. GET /api/_c/tokens/v1 Your tokens. Superusers see all, or one owner's with ?ownerCollection=&owner= . POST /api/_c/tokens/v1 {name, scopes, ttl \ expires} ( ttl in seconds, expires RFC 3339); superusers may add ownerCollection and owner . Returns the secret once. A scoped token can only create tokens within its own scopes. DELETE /api/_c/tokens/v1/{id} Revoke one. POST /api/_c/tokens/v1/revoke-all Revoke all of yours (superusers: {ownerCollection, owner} ). GET /api/_c/tokens/v1/scopes The registered scopes, who may own tokens, and whether you can. Owners can also list, view and delete their own tokens through the records API of _tokens .

title: Tokens
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens, the token API ( /api/_c/tokens/v1 ) and the token command. // Command example runs one PocketOne app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens in the dashboard, the token API (/api/_c/tokens/v1) // and the token command. // // go run ./example serve // go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci // curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_..." http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "net/http" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" tk := tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{ Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens }) // an extension's scope: a token limited to "hello" only authenticates under /api/hello; a JWT or unscoped token // holds it too, and every request that holds it carries X-Token-Scope-Hello: 1 for rules and hooks tk.MustRegisterScope(tokens.Scope{Name: "hello", Description: "Say hello", Paths: []string{"/api/hello"}, Methods: []string{"GET"}}) app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"hello": e.Auth.Email()}) }).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), tokens.RequireScope("hello")) return se.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Tokens
heading: Go config
text: tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{ Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens (default: every auth collection) MaxTTL: 0, // cap on a token's lifetime (0: none) }) With MaxTTL set, a token asked for with no expiry or a later one gets the cap instead. If you narrow Collections , The OAuth server can only sign in accounts of those collections.

title: Tokens
heading: How it works
text: Tokens live in the _tokens collection: owner (collection id and record id), name, hash (SHA-256 of the secret; the secret itself is never stored), display prefix, scopes, expiry, last use (time and IP), OAuth client id and audience. The bearer check is a middleware that runs just before PocketBase's own auth middleware; a second one, right after it, sets the scope headers. Last use is written at most once a minute per token. example/main.go runs one app where superusers and users may own tokens, with a hello scope for GET /api/hello . Try it with go run ./example serve and go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci (logins from devusers: admin@example.com / password, user@example.com / password).

title: Tokens
heading: License
text: MIT

title: OAuth
text: Tokens includes an OAuth 2.1 authorization server whose access tokens are API tokens: the oauth/v1 contract. pocketone login signs in to it in the browser (or with a code on another device), and MCP clients such as Claude or ChatGPT connectors register themselves and connect. Superusers and app users sign in on your app's own pages, through PocketBase's own auth endpoints.

title: OAuth
heading: Install
text: It comes with Tokens, which is in every app's standard set. There's nothing to install or turn on. Its endpoints are under /api/_c/oauth/v1/ (see Endpoints); its metadata is at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server . In your own Go build, configure it through Tokens: set := standard.New() set.Tokens = tokens.New(tokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{ Branding: tokens.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5"}, }}) tokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{Disabled: true}} leaves it out.

title: OAuth
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or environment variable for OAuth Server. In pocketone : superusers and every auth collection may sign in; access tokens last 30 days, refresh tokens 180 days (renewed on each refresh); tokens for MCP never expire, since MCP turns that on for /mcp ; client self-registration ( POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register ) is on, since MCP turns it on; Claude and Claude Code connect without registering (their client metadata documents from claude.ai and claude.com are trusted). A Go build can change these (see Go config).

title: OAuth
heading: Sign-in methods
text: The pages offer exactly the methods each auth collection has on, so you set them where you always do: the collection's options in the dashboard ( Collections → the collection → Options ). Password , One-time password (an emailed code) and OAuth2 providers each get their own form or button. Multi-factor authentication adds a second step. The collection's auth rule (for example verified = true ) applies. OAuth2 providers (Google, GitHub, …) are offered to app users only; PocketBase doesn't allow them for superusers. Register /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback as a redirect URI with each provider. The pages show Settings → Application → Application name .

title: OAuth
heading: Behind a proxy
text: The server names itself (the issuer) after the scheme and host the browser used, with https when the request is TLS or X-Forwarded-Proto says so. If a proxy rewrites the host, set Config.Issuer in a Go build so the issuer and the provider callback URL stay stable.

title: OAuth
heading: Scopes
text: A client may ask for any scope registered with Tokens, including your own from $tokens.registerScope . offline_access is accepted (refresh tokens are always issued). The consent page lets the user decide: Full access (no scopes: the account's full rights) or Only these , with a box for each scope. The scopes the client asked for start ticked; the others the account may hold are there to tick, except ones that only reach contract APIs under /api/_c/ (like deploy ), which appear only when asked for. With no scopes asked, Full access starts selected. The token gets exactly what was ticked, and the token response's scope says which.

title: OAuth
heading: Your own sign-in pages
text: The built-in pages (sign-in, second step, one-time code, consent, device code, done, error) follow the system's light or dark mode and work on phones. To change them, eject them as PocketPages templates: pocketone oauth eject # --force overwrites files you already have It writes signin.ejs , mfa.ejs , otp.ejs , consent.ejs , device.ejs , done.ejs , error.ejs and the shared head.ejs , foot.ejs and hidden.ejs (with the CSS) to pb_pages/_private/oauth/ , and prints each file. From then on the server renders your templates; a missing one falls back to the built-in page, so delete them to go back. _private keeps them from being served as routes. See Custom page templates for the data they get.

title: OAuth
heading: Signing in
text: Whenever a client sends someone to your app ( pocketone login , Claude, an app of yours), they see: Sign in to : the form for app users ( users first; with several user collections, a tab for each). At the bottom, Sign in as a superuser switches to the superuser form, which looks clearly different: a Superuser badge, Superuser sign-in , its own colors and a warning. Sign in as a user instead goes back. One more step when the account has MFA, offering its other methods. After a password, when an emailed code is the only method left, it's sent right away. Check your email for an emailed code. The consent page: the client's name, the account, whether the client will act as a user (and which collection) or as a superuser, and the access: Full access or Only these scopes (see Scopes). Click Allow or Deny , or Not ? Use another account . With no user collection allowed, the superuser form is the only one. A browser stays signed in to these pages for 15 minutes. Failed attempts are limited to 10 per IP in 5 minutes. On another device (over SSH, say), the client shows a code like WDJB-MJHT . Open https:// /api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify , enter it under Connect a device , sign in and allow. Codes last 10 minutes.

title: OAuth
heading: Log in from the command line
text: pocketone login prod With OAuth Server on the remote, Remotes opens your browser on the pages above, or shows a device code when there's no browser ( --device asks for one). The client is the built-in pocketone-cli , named pocketone CLI on the consent page (the name follows the command, so another build shows its own).

title: OAuth
heading: See and revoke what's connected
text: Every sign-in creates an API token named " (OAuth)". They're listed under Settings → API tokens with an oauth: label; click Revoke to disconnect a client. Revoking the access token also ends its refresh token. A client can revoke its own tokens at POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/revoke , which pocketone logout does.

title: OAuth
heading: Register clients
text: Claude and the CLI need no registration, and MCP clients register themselves. For your own app: pocketone oauth clients add --name "My app" --redirect https://myapp.example.com/callback pocketone oauth clients add --name "Desktop" --redirect http://127.0.0.1/callback --public pocketone oauth clients list pocketone oauth clients rm add prints the client id, and the secret once for a confidential client. --public makes a client with no secret (PKCE only), for desktop and mobile apps. --redirect can be repeated. Redirect URIs must be https , http on a loopback address, or an app's custom scheme. Loopback URIs match any port (RFC 8252); others must match exactly.

title: OAuth
heading: In the logs
text: tokens: oauth: this collection may sign in but can't own API tokens; add it to tokens.Config.Collections , once per collection, when Tokens is narrowed in a Go build. The page then says signing in with that account type "isn't set up on this server yet". tokens: oauth: auth methods (error) when a collection's sign-in methods can't be read. tokens: oauth: cleanup (warning) when the half-hourly removal of expired codes fails.

title: OAuth
heading: Works with
text: Tokens It's part of Tokens. Access tokens are API tokens owned by whoever signed in, with the client's id, the granted scopes and the audience. Every registered scope can be requested. Remotes remote/v1's whoami lists oauth/v1 (and the oauth feature, its metadata); pocketone login then signs in in the browser (loopback redirect with PKCE) or with a device code, and renews through the refresh token. MCP MCP points clients here from its protected resource metadata, turns on self-registration, and makes tokens bound to /mcp never expire. Tool calls run as whoever signed in. Deploy pocketone login gives the deploy commands a token for the account that signed in. Pages pocketone oauth eject writes the pages as PocketPages templates, rendered from then on. Under Pocker every instance has it, through the standard set.

title: OAuth
heading: Audience (RFC 8707)
text: A resource parameter on /api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize , /api/_c/oauth/v1/device or /api/_c/oauth/v1/token (a URL on this server) binds the access token to it: the token then only works under that URL's path. So a token issued for /mcp can't deploy, and a deploy token can't drive MCP. Refreshed tokens keep it.

title: OAuth
heading: Building on the OAuth server
text: Go API. tokens.OAuth(app) returns the server. Issuer(e) is its public base URL; EnableDynamicRegistration() turns on POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register ; SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0) sets the lifetime of tokens bound to a resource (0: never expire). FindClient , ListClients , AddClient and RemoveClient manage clients. Scopes. Register a scope with Tokens (Go or $tokens.registerScope ) and clients can ask for it; nothing else is needed. Render the pages yourself. Config.Render(e, page, data) renders any page (return handled=false to fall back), with PageData . It wins over ejected templates.

title: OAuth
heading: Example
text: The OAuth server is on wherever Tokens is (its example runs it). To brand it and let MCP connectors register themselves: set := standard.New() set.Tokens = tokens.New(tokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{ DynamicRegistration: true, // MCP connectors register themselves (ext/mcp turns this on anyway) Branding: tokens.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Example OAuth server"}, }}) app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{})

title: OAuth
heading: Endpoints
text: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server Metadata (RFC 8414). The issuer is Config.Issuer , else the request's own scheme and host. GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/authorize Sign-in and consent pages. Authorization code with PKCE (S256 only; required). POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/token authorization_code , refresh_token and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code . Refresh rotates without logouts: the old access token lives out its time, and the old refresh token works again for 2 minutes, so two processes refreshing at once both succeed. POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/device , GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/device/verify Device flow (RFC 8628): codes like WDJB-MJHT , valid 10 minutes. POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/revoke Revocation (RFC 7009): an access token or a refresh token (revokes both). GET/POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback Where OAuth2 providers send the browser back after sign-in. POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), when DynamicRegistration is on or an extension called EnableDynamicRegistration() (MCP does). Public clients by default. Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) belongs to the resource: MCP serves /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource .

title: OAuth
heading: Clients
text: pocketone-cli is built in: public, any http://127.0.0.1: /… or [::1] redirect, device codes. It's what pocketone login uses. Client ID metadata documents (CIMD): an https:// client id is fetched as a JSON document ( client_id must equal the URL; its client_name and redirect_uris are used; public clients only; cached 10 minutes). Only Config.CIMDHosts are trusted (default claude.ai , claude.com ); the metadata says client_id_metadata_document_supported . Registered clients live in _tokens_oauth_clients ; codes, device codes and refresh tokens in _tokens_oauth_codes .

title: OAuth
heading: How sign-in works
text: The pages never check passwords or codes themselves. Each step calls PocketBase's own auth endpoint in-process, through the app's router, so the collection's auth rule, MFA, rate limits, superuser IP limits and every onRecordAuth Request hook apply as for the REST API, and the record the endpoint returns is the one signed in: password: POST /api/collections/{c}/auth-with-password ; emailed code: POST …/request-otp , then POST …/auth-with-otp ; OAuth2: the browser goes to the provider with the state and PKCE from GET …/auth-methods , comes back to /api/_c/oauth/v1/provider/callback , and POST …/auth-with-oauth2 completes it (account linking and sign-up are PocketBase's); MFA: when an auth call answers 401 with an mfaId , the second page passes it along. Only collections with a sign-in method on are offered. Access tokens are owned by the signed-in record, so every collection that may sign in must also be allowed by Tokens (its default is every auth collection). The session is a 15-minute HttpOnly cookie on /api/_c/oauth/v1 ; forms carry a CSRF token; a provider round trip keeps its state in a signed 10-minute cookie.

title: OAuth
heading: Go config
text: tokens.New(tokens.Config{OAuth: tokens.OAuthConfig{ Collections: nil, // who may sign in; default: _superusers + every auth collection AccessTTL: 30 24 time.Hour, // default; per resource with srv.SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0) RefreshTTL: 180 24 time.Hour, // default, renewed on each refresh DynamicRegistration: false, // POST /api/_c/oauth/v1/register (MCP turns it on) CIMDHosts: nil, // default claude.ai, claude.com; an empty non-nil slice turns CIMD off Issuer: "", // public base URL; default: the request's scheme and host Branding: tokens.Branding{LogoURL: "/logo.svg", Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Acme Inc."}, }}) Branding also takes a Name (default: Settings → Application name). Accent is the button color (default #16161a ).

title: OAuth
heading: Custom page templates
text: Ejected templates get ctx.data : PageData in camelCase ( data.appName , data.action , data.hidden , data.csrf , data.clientName , data.scopes , data.scopeChoices , data.superuser , data.providers , data.error , …). Every POST form must include include('/oauth/hidden') and a step button. Steps: password , request_otp , otp , oauth2: , use: (switch forms; use: is the default user form), allow , deny , switch . Sign-in forms post collection ; the MFA and code pages also post mfa_id / otp_id . Consent posts access = full , or limited with a grant field per ticked scope (from data.scopeChoices : name , description , checked ). A consent form without access grants what the client asked for.

heading: License
text: MIT

title: Upgrade
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @benallfree pocketone upgrade replaces the pocketone executable with the latest PocketOne release and keeps the old one beside it as - (for example pocketone-0.0.3 ), so a project can keep running the engine it was built with. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Upgrade
heading: Install
text: Upgrade is built into pocketone : the upgrade command is always there. There's nothing to turn on. In your own Go build, register the command before the app starts: import "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/upgrade" app := pocketbase.New() upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{}) app.Start()

title: Upgrade
heading: Configure
text: Nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, no environment variables, no settings screens. The command has one flag: --backup true Back up pb_data after upgrading, if the current folder has one. --backup=false skips it. --yes , -y false Move from a stable release to a prerelease without asking.

title: Upgrade
heading: Use
text: Run it from your project folder: pocketone upgrade It: Picks the newest release on GitHub that fits what you're running, and stops if you already have it: The newest release is offered, prereleases included: 0.1.0-alpha.2 goes to 0.1.0-alpha.3 or 0.1.0 , whichever is newest. From one prerelease to the next (or to a stable release), it just upgrades. From a stable release to a prerelease ( 0.1.0 to 0.1.1-alpha.1 ), it asks first. No means the newest stable release instead, if there's a newer one. --yes answers yes for you; with no answer (no terminal), it's no. A local build upgrades to the newest release without asking. Downloads the archive for your platform and checks it against the release's checksums.txt before touching anything. Renames the current executable to - and puts the new one in its place. Old copies are never deleted , so pocketone-0.0.3 serve still runs a project on that version. A local build with no release version is kept as .old , which the next such upgrade replaces. Backs up pb_data , when the current folder has one, as @upgrade_ .zip in PocketBase's backups. Prints the new version, where the old one was kept, and the release notes. Two cases where it does something else: Installed with Homebrew: it prints brew upgrade pocketone instead. Homebrew keeps the previous version until brew cleanup . In a Docker container: it refuses; upgrade the image instead. It needs write access to the folder the executable is in. A kept executable doesn't undo migrations: once a newer version has served a pb_data , an older one may not open it. The backup is the way back for that.

title: Upgrade
heading: Integrations
text: Nothing integrates with it yet. Other tools can reuse its release code: Custom builds that publish their own releases set Owner , Repo , ArchivePrefix and ArchiveExecutable in upgrade.Config . Release archives are named _ _ _ .zip , with a goreleaser-style checksums.txt in the same release. Go API. Config.FetchReleases(ctx) lists the published releases, prereleases included, and upgrade.UpgradeFor(current, releases, stableOnly) picks the one to upgrade to and upgrade.NeedsConfirm(current, release) says whether to ask first. Config.FetchRelease(ctx, tag) fetches GitHub's latest stable release (tag "" ) or a given one; Config.DownloadArchive(ctx, release, goos, goarch, dir) downloads and checks a platform's archive. upgrade.KeptName(exe, version) is the name an old executable is kept under.

title: Upgrade
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is a PocketOne app with just the upgrade command. Try it with go run ./example upgrade . // Command example is a PocketOne app with just the upgrade command. A local build has no release version, so it is // kept as "example.old"; release builds are kept as " - ". // // go run ./example upgrade package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/upgrade" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }
