title: WASM
text: Version 0.0.1 · Owners: @octavonu Bring your own WASM (BYOW). Your own code, in Go, Rust, Zig or anything that builds for WASI, in pb_hooks, where $os.cmd and $os.exec aren't allowed: a plugin is a small program compiled to WebAssembly that your hooks call like a function. Input in, output out, or an error. It can't reach the database, files, network, environment or other processes; your hook gives it what it needs and decides what to do with the result. // pb_hooks/main.pb.js onRecordCreate((e) = { const out = $wasm.run("summary", { title: e.record.get("title"), body: e.record.get("body") }) e.record.set("summary", out.text) e.next() }, "posts") Use it for what JS hooks do badly or slowly: parsing (EDIFACT, XML, binary formats), crypto, validation, number crunching, or a library that only exists in Go, Rust or C. WASM is an extension; the .wasm files it runs are plugins. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: WASM
heading: Install
text: WASM isn't built into pocketone yet. In your own build, add it to the standard set, which every app and every pocker instance gets; the set binds $wasm into the JS engine ( ext/jsvm ): set := standard.New().Add(wasm.New(wasm.Config{})) // $wasm in pb_hooks Without the set, register it and bind it yourself: p := wasm.New(wasm.Config{}) app := pocketbase.New() extkit.MustRegister(app, p) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, p) }}) app.Start() $wasm needs PocketOne's JS engine; with PocketBase's own ( --jsvm goja ) extensions bind nothing. The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/wasm . Plugins load from pb_wasm/ , beside pb_data/ and pb_hooks/ ; nothing else needs setting up.

title: WASM
heading: Configure
text: The defaults suit most apps. To change them, pass them to wasm.New : Dir pb_wasm beside the data dir The plugin folder. MaxCallMemoryMB 32 Memory each call may allocate (its heap, stack and input). Every call has its own, not shared: 8 calls at once may take 8 × 32 MB. A call that needs more crashes alone. Timeout 5s Time limit for a call's run (compiling comes before it). MaxConcurrent 8 Calls running at once in the app. More wait, up to Timeout , then fail as busy . MaxModulesMB 10 MB of plugin modules running at once: the .wasm sizes of the calls running, added up (file sizes, not memory). More wait, as above. It's also the largest module that runs. MaxPayload 4 MB Largest input or output of a call. There's no pocketone.yaml section. Under pocker, each instance can override these (see Integrations).

title: WASM
heading: Plugins are files
text: A plugin is pb_wasm/ .wasm , with an optional pb_wasm/ .json . The app creates pb_wasm/ when it starts, if it isn't there (on a disk it can't write to, it only logs that and serves with no plugins): pb_hooks/main.pb.js pb_wasm/summary.wasm pb_wasm/summary.json It ships with the rest of your code: git, pocketone deploy (which sends every pb_ folder), or SFTP. Like node script.js , every call reads the plugin's files as they are then, so a plugin added, changed or removed takes effect on the next call, with no restart. To turn a plugin off, remove or rename its .wasm . Hidden files and files that don't end in .wasm are ignored, so upload a new version under a hidden name ( .summary.wasm.part ) and rename it over the old one: no call reads it half written. A plugin that can't run (a broken module, a bad .json , a module over MaxModulesMB ) fails its calls with not_loaded and says why, and $wasm.plugins() says it too; the other plugins run as usual. .json is optional, and so is each of its fields: { "description": "Summarizes a post: its title and first words, and a word count", "version": "1.2.0", "functions": ["run"], "language": "Rust", "repository": "https://github.com/you/summary", "examples": [ { "function": "run", "input": {"title": "Hello", "body": "one two three"}, "output": {"text": "Hello: one two three", "words": 3} } ] } description what it does version the author's version, as you write it ( 1.2.0 , 2026-11-15 ): up to 32 letters, digits and .+_- ; only shown functions the functions hooks may call (default ["run"] ) language what it's written in, shown when the module doesn't say: a Go module always does, a Rust one unless it's stripped ( strip = true ), a Zig one never repository where its source is: an http(s) URL (no javascript: , no credentials), at most 256 characters examples up to 16 calls to try it with: function (default run ), input (a JSON string is the plugin's stdin as it is, anything else goes as JSON, as with $wasm.run ) and, optionally, the output it gives Nothing runs the examples, reads the version or language, or fetches the repository: they're shown by $wasm.plugins() , for people and for tests (run each example and compare its output). An example works the same locally: printf '%s' '{"title":"Hello","body":"one two three"}' wazero run summary.wasm run . Any other field is refused: a plugin can't ask for anything, so a manifest that expects more (dependencies, permissions) doesn't run without it. A manifest is at most 64 KB.

title: WASM
heading: Calling from pb_hooks
text: $wasm.run(name, input) // the plugin's "run" $wasm.call(name, function, input) // one of the functions its .json declares $wasm.plugins() // [{name, running, description, version, functions, language, repository, examples, // size, error}] $wasm.limits() // {maxCallMemoryMB, timeoutMs, maxConcurrent, maxModulesMB, maxPayload} $wasm.inspect(name, function, input) // {output, stderr, error, compileMs, runMs}, for trying a plugin out await $wasm.run.async(name, input) // the same, off the app's JS VM; also $wasm.call.async, $wasm.inspect.async The input is the plugin's stdin: a string or bytes (an ArrayBuffer , a Uint8Array or another typed array) as they are, nothing for undefined or null , anything else as JSON. So $wasm.run("edifact", e.record.get("raw")) hands over the raw text, byte for byte. The output is the plugin's stdout: parsed if it's JSON, a string if not, null if empty. A failed call throws an Error named WasmError , with code , message , retryable and plugin : try { e.record.set("summary", $wasm.run("summary", post).text) } catch (err) { if (err.name !== "WasmError" err.code !== "empty_body") throw err } not_found no .wasm in the folder not_loaded in the folder, but it can't run (the message says why: a broken module, a bad .json , too large), or the app isn't serving no_such_function the function isn't in its .json timeout over the time limit (retryable) crashed it trapped, panicked or ran out of memory too_large input or output over the limit busy the calls running left no room for this one (retryable); the message gives the numbers plugin_error it exited non-zero without a code of its own anything else the plugin's own code (below) $wasm.inspect makes the same call but never throws for it: it returns the output (or null ), the error as {code, message, retryable} (or null ), what the plugin wrote to stderr (up to 64 KB), and how long compiling and running took. It's for pages that let a superuser try a plugin out; hooks use run and call . The JS engine runs one VM per app, and run and call hold it while the plugin compiles and runs: the app's other hooks and requests wait. That's fine for a plugin that answers in milliseconds (Rust, Zig). For a slow one (a Go plugin compiles for over a second each call) or many calls at once, use .async in an async hook, so the app serves other requests meanwhile: onRecordCreate(async (e) = { const out = await $wasm.run.async("summary", { title: e.record.get("title"), body: e.record.get("body") }) e.record.set("summary", out.text) return e.next() }, "posts") The time limit covers the run; compiling comes before it (below). $wasm is declared in each app's pb_data/types.d.ts ( wasm.d.ts ), for code completion and tsc .

title: WASM
heading: Writing a plugin
text: A plugin is a plain WASI program ( wasip1 ), the way you'd write a command-line tool: read stdin, write stdout, exit. The function asked for is its first argument ( os.Args[1] , "run" for $wasm.run ). To fail, exit non-zero; if stderr is a JSON object {"code", "message", "retryable"} , hooks get it as is, any other text becomes the message of a plugin_error . Anything it writes to stderr on success goes to the app's log (Logs in the dashboard), so stderr is its log. Go ( example/summary ): func main() { var post struct{ Title, Body string } if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&post); err != nil { fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, {"code":"bad_input","message":"not a post"} ) os.Exit(1) } json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]any{"text": post.Title, "words": len(strings.Fields(post.Body))}) } GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_wasm/summary.wasm . Rust ( example/summary-rust ): a binary crate, serde for JSON. rustup target add wasm32-wasip1 # once cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 Zig ( example/summary-zig ): an executable for wasm32-wasi . Set stack_size = 1 << 20 in build.zig : Zig's default stack is 16 MB, and every call would start with it. Any language that builds a WASI program works the same way (C, TinyGo, AssemblyScript with WASI, ...). Try a plugin without an app: echo '{"title":"Hi","body":"one two"}' wazero run summary.wasm run . Two things are refused when the plugin loads, with a message that says so: a library instead of a program: Go's -buildmode=c-shared , or any module without _start ("not a WASI program"); a module that imports anything outside wasi_snapshot_preview1 , such as an Extism plugin built with its PDK, or host functions this host doesn't have.

title: WASM
heading: Which language
text: Go 4.4 MB 240 ms 1.7 s ~20–30 MB + 3.6 MB Rust 95 KB 37 ms 39 ms ~2–5 MB + 1.1 MB Zig 55 KB 39 ms 23 ms ~2.5 MB + 1.2 MB Every call compiles the plugin from scratch and runs it, and nothing compiled is kept: a plugin takes memory only while a call runs, however many plugins the apps have: between calls, nothing. The compiled code is most of it; the program's own memory (its stack and heap, Go's runtime and garbage collector included) stays under MaxCallMemoryMB . Compiling is almost all of a call's time: the summary itself runs in a few milliseconds. Measured on a laptop (2026-11-14), one call at a time; the compiled code's size is approximate, and a Go plugin's varies with what it imports (one that imports net/http is ~11 MB). Go calls compiling at once also slow each other down: one took +19 MB, two +38 MB, four +245 MB (2026-11-16). That's why the calls running at once are limited by their modules' size, MaxModulesMB , and not only by their number. An admin picks the trade-off with that one number: 5 1 8 ( MaxConcurrent ) ~25 MB 10 (default) 2 8 ~45 MB 20 4 8 ~250 MB Pick by what the plugin does. Go is the easiest to write and fine where a call can take a second or two (a cron job, an import, an admin action). A plugin on a hot path (every record save, every request) is better in Rust or Zig, whose calls are 40 times faster and take a seventh of the memory.

title: WASM
heading: Works with
text: Pocker One extension value serves every instance (the standard set). Each instance has its own plugins, in its own pb_wasm/ , its own call slots and limits. Each call reads the instance's pb_wasm/ as it is then; nothing runs between calls (below). Sandbox $wasm is safe to give a hostile tenant: a plugin gets nothing but its input. A call can't be interrupted by the JS engine's time limits, so Timeout (and compiling) bound it instead. Deploy pocketone deploy sends pb_wasm/ with the other pb_ folders; the next call of each plugin runs the new version, with no restart.

title: WASM
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: Each instance can override maxCallMemoryMB , maxConcurrent , maxModulesMB , timeout (a duration, like 5s ) and maxPayload in its extensions.wasm settings, over the Config given to New , key by key. enabled: false turns $wasm off for that instance ( typeof $wasm === "undefined" in its hooks). A change restarts just that instance, on its next request: instances: id: abc extensions: { wasm: { timeout: 10s, maxCallMemoryMB: 64 } } id: no-plugins extensions: { wasm: { enabled: false } } Leave dir unset there: each instance then gets the pb_wasm/ in its own folder. MaxConcurrent and MaxModulesMB count per instance, so one instance's busy plugins never make another's calls wait. A restart (new settings, a pb_hooks change, a restore) lets calls in progress finish, and the instance's plugins run as before after it, from its folder: nothing to reload.

title: WASM
heading: Building on WASM
text: There's no Go API, endpoint or form for calling a plugin: pb_hooks ( $wasm ) are the only way in, so whatever reaches a plugin went through the app's own code.

title: WASM
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with a posts collection and the hook above; its folder is laid out like an instance ( pb_data/ , pb_hooks/ , pb_wasm/ ). Build the plugin into example/pb_wasm/ , then cd example && go run . serve --dev and create a post. // Command example runs one app with ext/wasm and the summary plugin wired in from pb_hooks: a new post gets its // summary before it's saved (pb_hooks/main.pb.js). The example folder is the app's folder, laid out like an // instance on PocketHost: pb_data/, pb_hooks/ and pb_wasm/ side by side. // // cd example && go run . serve --dev // // Build the plugin into pb_wasm/ (before or after starting the app: each call reads it): // // mkdir -p pb_wasm && cp summary/plugin.json pb_wasm/summary.json // (cd summary && GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o ../pb_wasm/summary.wasm .) // // Then create a post (dashboard, or the API) and look at its summary field. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit/js" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/wasm" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" app.OnBootstrap().BindFunc(func(e core.BootstrapEvent) error { if err := e.Next(); err != nil { return err } return posts(e.App) }) // the same extension value the standard set gives every pocker instance (set.Add(wasm.New(...))) plugins := wasm.New(wasm.Config{}) extkit.MustRegister(app, plugins) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: "pb_hooks", OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, plugins) }, // $wasm in pb_hooks }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } func posts(app core.App) error { if _, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts"); err == nil { return nil } c := core.NewBaseCollection("posts") c.Fields.Add(&core.TextField{Name: "title"}, &core.TextField{Name: "body", Max: 100000}, &core.TextField{Name: "summary", Max: 1000}, &core.NumberField{Name: "words"}) return app.Save(c) }

title: WASM
heading: More example plugins
text: Each is a plain program with a plugin.json (its functions and examples, so /wasm -style pages and the wazero CLI can try it), built with the command in its header. They answer the usual questions about a feature like this: summary , summary-rust , summary-zig Go, Rust, Zig The same plugin in three languages: the hook above, and how much the language matters (a Go module is ~4 MB and compiles for over a second; Rust and Zig, under 100 KB and ~40 ms). crypto Go What an app used to run with $os.exec : AES-256-GCM. The key comes in with each call; the plugin can't keep it or send it anywhere. waflows Rust What pb_hooks can't do: a WhatsApp Flows endpoint needs RSA-OAEP and AES-GCM with WhatsApp's key and IV. The hook keeps the JSON and HTTP; the plugin does only those two. edifact-orders-rust Rust A real format with a real library (edifact-rs): an EDIFACT ORDERS message, as raw text, read into an order. order-xml Rust The same order from XML (roxmltree), so a hook takes either format and stores one shape. devil Rust Is it safe? It tries, in plain sight, to read the app's database and /etc/passwd , list folders, write a file, read the environment, run sh -c id and send to attacker.example . Every try says refused . memhog Rust What does it cost? It asks for more memory than MaxCallMemoryMB : that call fails as crashed , saying which limit it hit, and the app goes on. probe shows the limit from inside.

title: WASM
heading: What a plugin can't do
text: Plugins run in wazero (pure Go, no cgo), in the app's process, with only the standard WASI functions and nothing behind them: No files: nothing is mounted, not even pb_wasm/ . open fails. No network: WASI preview 1 has no way to connect. (Go's net on wasip1 is an in-memory stand-in: a plugin can "listen", but nothing outside the program reaches it.) No environment, no processes , no arguments beyond the function name. No state between calls: every call gets a fresh instance, so nothing from one call (or one caller) reaches the next. Bounded: memory, time, input and output size, and how many calls run at once (see Configure). It does get a real clock and real random numbers (crypto nonces need them). Data from the app, secrets and API responses reach a plugin only as input from your hook, and the result goes nowhere but back to the hook: the network stays with $http.send in pb_hooks.

title: WASM
heading: How it works
text: Plugins run only while the app serves (other commands, such as migrate , never read them, nor create the folder). Like node script.js : each call reads its plugin's files ( .json , then .wasm once the call has room), compiles the module in a wazero runtime of its own, runs it, and closes it after. Nothing stays in memory between calls, so a folder of 100 plugins costs nothing while they aren't called, and no compilation cache, in memory or on disk. Compiling validates the module: a broken or half-written one doesn't run. A call in progress finishes with what it read, whatever happens to the file meanwhile. Compiling counts toward MaxConcurrent and MaxModulesMB , so the memory it takes stays bounded too. Nothing watches the folder: no inotify watches (Linux allows only 128 per user by default, and pocker runs many apps in one process), no timer, no work between calls, however many instances there are. $wasm.plugins() lists the folder each time. It checks each module with wazero's interpreter, which validates it without making machine code (~180 ms for a Go plugin), and keeps only what it found (manifest, language, error) until the plugin's files change size or time; when the app starts serving, it checks them all once, so the log says which ones can't run. A call waits for room: fewer than MaxConcurrent calls running, and its module's size left in MaxModulesMB ( $wasm.plugins() gives each one's size ). Compiling takes time and memory in step with a module's size, so with the defaults (8 calls, 10 MB) a Rust or Zig plugin (~0.1 MB) runs 8 calls at once and a Go one (~4.4 MB) 2, beside small ones. A call goes in as soon as there's room for it, so a small call doesn't queue behind a big one that's waiting; under a steady stream of small calls, a big one may wait until it gives up as busy . No collection and no database use: what's in the folder, and why a plugin can't run, comes from the files ( $wasm.plugins() and the log).

text: MIT

title: Installation
text: PocketOne is one executable, pocketone . It is built on PocketBase v0.41 and takes the same commands and flags, plus its own.

title: Installation
heading: Homebrew (macOS and Linux)
text: brew install pockethost/tap/pocketone The formula lives in pockethost/homebrew-tap.

title: Installation
heading: Download a release
text: Download the zip for your platform from Releases, unzip it, and put pocketone somewhere on your PATH .

title: Installation
heading: Build from source
text: With Go installed: git clone https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone.git cd pocketone/examples/pocketone go build -o pocketone .

title: Installation
heading: Run it
text: Create your first superuser before the first serve: pocketone superuser upsert pocketone serve Opening http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/ to create it also works, as in PocketBase. To start a site with server-rendered pages: pocketone pages create myapp cd myapp pocketone serve --dev --dir ./pb_data In dev mode ( serve --dev ), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send mail through the system's sendmail . PocketOne catches the mail and shows it at http://127.0.0.1:8025 .

title: Installation
heading: Upgrade
text: pocketone upgrade This replaces the executable with the latest release. The old one is kept beside it as pocketone- , never deleted, so you can go back.

title: Installation
heading: Moving from PocketBase
text: PocketOne reads the same pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public folders. Point it at your existing data directory with --dir , as you would with pocketbase . Back up pb_data first.

title: What is PocketOne?
text: PocketOne is a community fork of PocketBase. It tracks upstream PocketBase and keeps its own changes to the core small: only the hooks that let extensions extend and override PocketBase. Every feature lives in an extension. It's maintained by PocketHost, which runs it in production. PocketOne is not affiliated with or endorsed by the PocketBase project.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: How it's built
text: A small core. PocketBase's own code changes only to add hooks. Each change is marked in the source, reviewed by someone who didn't write it, and kept minimal so upstream releases merge cleanly. Everything else is an extension. Extensions live in ext/ in the repo. Each is its own Go module, with a README and a small example. Off until you use it. The extensions in the pocketone binary add no work to an app that doesn't use them. One app or hundreds. An extension written against the extension contract works the same on a single app and on every instance under a multi-instance host.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Open to contributions
text: PocketOne is open to everyone. Ask questions and share ideas in GitHub Discussions, report bugs in Issues, and send extensions as pull requests. Start with Writing an extension.

title: What is PocketOne?
heading: Where to next
text: Install PocketOne See what PocketOne adds to PocketBase Browse the extensions

title: PocketBase docs
text: PocketOne doesn't change how PocketBase itself works, so its docs are the reference for everything outside the extensions. This site doesn't copy them. Introduction Collections API rules and filters Authentication Files upload and handling Working with relations Extend with JavaScript Extend with Go Going to production Web APIs reference PocketOne is built on PocketBase v0.41. When the docs there describe a newer release, some of it may not be in PocketOne yet.

title: What PocketOne adds
text: Run pocketone the way you run pocketbase . These are the differences you'll notice.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Point-in-time restore, on by default
text: Your database is replicated with Litestream, so you can restore it to any moment from Settings → Backups or with pocketone pitr restore . Turn it off with --pitr=false .

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Mail you can see in dev mode
text: In dev mode ( serve --dev ), an app with no SMTP settings doesn't send through the system's sendmail . The mail is caught and shown at http://127.0.0.1:8025 .

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Server-rendered pages
text: Put .ejs and Markdown files in a pb_pages folder and they're served as pages, with no build step. This site is one. pocketone pages create myapp starts a new site from a starter kit. Full docs are at pocketpages.dev.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: A config file
text: Settings can live in pocketone.yaml , with secrets in a .env file beside it that your JS hooks never see. Without the file, PocketOne behaves like stock PocketBase. pocketone config lists every section, and pocketone config check checks a file. The config reference lists every section.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Commands for working with remote apps
text: pocketone login , remote and link : save logins to your apps. pocketone deploy , dev , pull and logs : ship pb_hooks , pb_migrations and pb_public to an app and watch it. pocketone upgrade : move to the latest release, keeping the old executable.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Agents and API tokens
text: An MCP endpoint at /mcp lets agents such as Claude manage your app and call its tools. Long-lived API tokens ( pbt_… ) with scopes, for scripts and integrations. Your app can act as an OAuth provider; pocketone login and MCP sign-in use it.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Extensions that fit together
text: PocketOne's extensions meet through contracts: named, versioned promises like restore/v1 that any extension can keep. The dashboard, the pocketone command, agents and your pb_hooks call the contract, so you can swap the extension behind it without changing anything else. How PocketOne fits together explains it.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: Everything else
text: Automatic TLS certificates, bulk mail to your own users, scheduled VACUUM, signed S3 download redirects, and more. See all extensions.

title: What PocketOne adds
heading: What stays the same
text: The admin dashboard, collections, rules, the REST and realtime APIs, JS hooks and migrations all work as in PocketBase. For those, the PocketBase docs are the reference.

title: Create your own extension
text: A PocketOne extension is Go code compiled into your build. There are two kinds, by where they run: App extensions add to an app: Go routes, PocketBase hooks, collections, admin dashboard screens, a JS API for pb_hooks , contracts other extensions use. They run on every app: a standalone app, or each instance of a multisite host. Almost every extension is one. Host extensions add to a multisite host, the process that serves many instances: request gates (firewall, rate limits), TLS, middleware around every instance, instance sources, background jobs. How a multisite host runs its instances (in-process with pocker, in containers with docker, or both) is the host's runtime/v1 contract. App extensions don't depend on it.

title: Create your own extension
heading: App extensions: extkit
text: Write an extension once, against extkit (its own module, github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit ; core has no part in it), and the same value runs on every app: type Extension struct{ cfg Config } func New(cfg Config) Extension { return &Extension{cfg: cfg} } func (p Extension) Name() string { return "hello" } // config key, _hello_ collections, logs func (p Extension) Register(app core.App, cfg extkit.Config) error { c := p.cfg if err := cfg.Decode(&c); err != nil { // this app's settings over the defaults (json tags) return err } app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { / routes, UI extensions / return se.Next() }) return nil } // optional: a $hello global in the app's JS hooks func (p Extension) BindJS(app core.App, rt js.Runtime) { / rt.Set("$hello", ...) / } // optional: its TypeScript declarations, added to each app's pb_data/types.d.ts func (p Extension) TypeScript() string { return declare var $hello: { greet(name: string): string }; } Every app has the standard set (tokens, mcp, pitr, deploy and the rest). Add yours to it: set.Add(myextension.New(...)) . On a standalone app, build the app with set.NewApp(...) , or build it yourself and call set.Register(app, jsvm.Config{...}) . The stock binary does the second: pocketbase.NewWithConfig , then set.Register ( examples/pocketone ). Without the set: extkit.MustRegister(app, extensions...) , and extkit.BindJS(app, vm, extensions...) in jsvm's OnInit . On a multisite host every instance gets the set, with that instance's extensions. settings over your constructor's defaults. enabled: false there means Register and BindJS are never called for that instance. What runs inside an instance depends on its runtime: pocker registers the set in-process; a docker instance runs the pocketone binary in its container, so it has the stock set (your own extras need your own image); an instance on a stock PocketBase image runs none, and gets only the contracts the host provides for it (Working together). Routes: an extension has none of its own. Its API is contracts, mounted for you under /api/_c/ / ; design the contract in ext/contracts first (Working together). Admin settings go through settings/v1 ( settingsv1.Add ). Only paths a standard fixes stay at the root ( /.well-known/ , /mcp ). The conformance test fails any other route unless conformance.Options.AllowRoutes lists it with a reason. Process-wide settings come from a pocketone.yaml section your extension owns ( extkit.NewSection ). State per app: keep it in app.Store() . Something shared across apps (a pool, a client) closes through extkit.Closer . Name the command with extkit.Command : when a message tells people what to run ("run 'pocketone login prod'"), build it from extkit.Command (default pocketone ), never a literal. A build shipped under another name (PocketHost's, say) sets it once in main , or with -ldflags "-X github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit.Command=pockethost" . bulkmail is the reference implementation, and ext/standard/example a complete program.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Working together: contracts
text: Start with How PocketOne fits together for the idea: every API an extension offers is a named, versioned contract, any extension can provide one, and everything else (the dashboard, the CLI, agents, pb_hooks , other extensions) calls the contract, never the extension. This section is how to do it in code. In short, when you design an extension: Find the contracts you need in the catalogue. Use them; don't reach into another extension. Decide what you offer. Anything a client calls is a contract. If one already promises it, provide that one (your extension then stands in for the current provider). If not, write the contract first, named for what it does, not for your extension. Declare it in Contracts() and provide it in Register . The startup lines, whoami and the catalogue show it from then on. Extensions never depend on each other by name. They depend on contracts : versioned Go interfaces in ext/contracts , such as deploy/v1 or mail.fallback/v1 . Every API an extension offers is a contract too, served at /api/_c/ / : extensions have no routes of their own. Every contract, standard or community, lives in ext/contracts/ /vN/ with a README like an extension's (owners and a one-line summary in its front matter; ## Use , ## Provide , ## Extensions , ## License ). Its Extensions section is generated from every extension's Contracts() : who provides it, requires it and works with it ( go run ./.github/extensions contracts ; CI fails when it's stale or when an extension names a contract that doesn't exist). Whoever first creates a contract owns it, so an extension author who adds one owns both. Design the contract first, then the extension that provides it. An extension declares what it implements, requires and works with: func (e Extension) Contracts() extkit.Contracts { return extkit.Contracts{ Implements: extkit.IDs("deploy/v1"), Defaults: extkit.IDs("deploy/v1"), // steps aside if another extension provides it WorksWith: extkit.IDs("tokens/v1"), // used when present } } func (e Extension) Register(app core.App, cfg extkit.Config) error { deployv1.Contract.ProvideDefault(app, myDeployer{}) return nil } At startup PocketOne resolves every contract and prints who provides it: standard: deploy/v1 ← fastdeploy (default deploy stepped aside) standard: bulkmail off: needs mail.fallback/v1, which nothing provides Look contracts up after registration (in hooks, at serve time): deployv1.Contract.Must(app) . A lookup inside Register panics. Defaults, conflicts, choices. A default steps aside for any other provider. Two other providers of a contract that allows one fail the start until pocketone.yaml picks one ( providers: { mail.fallback/v1: mailrelay } ). Wrappers decorate whatever provides a contract ( Contract.Wrap ), in registration order. Wire contracts have an HTTP API at /api/_c/ / , action hooks in Go ( deployv1.OnUpload ) and JS ( onDeployUpload ), an MCP tool per operation and a client. Every caller passes the same scope check and hooks. From pb_hooks: an app's JS declares and provides its contracts in onContracts , which runs once after pb_hooks load and before the seal (so before bootstrap): onContracts((e) = { e.provide("mail.fallback/v1", { send(m) { / ... / } }) // a contract open to JS e.require("restore/v1") // the start fails (dev mode: warns) when nothing provides it e.worksWith("tokens/v1") // shown in the startup lines e.next() }) The startup lines show it ( pb_hooks: provides mail.fallback/v1; requires restore/v1 ). Methods run on pooled runtimes like any hook handler, so they can't use the file's local variables. A Go extension that requires a contract only JS provides is resolved before the JS runs: name pb_hooks under providers: for it in pocketone.yaml . CLI: every operation of a wire contract is a pocketone remote ... command with no code ( remote restore to --at -2h ), flags from its input. Provide cli.commands/v1 to replace one with your own, or to add one ( remote rehash ). No imports between extensions. An extension imports extkit and contract packages, never another extension's module (tests and examples may). What it needs from another goes in the contract package: tokens/v1 has RegisterScope , FromRequest and WithScopes ; remote/v1 has its CLI client ( remoteclient ), which deploy's commands use.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Compiled in, not loaded at run time
text: Extensions are Go packages linked into the binary, the way Caddy modules work. Go's plugin package ( .so files) isn't used: it needs identical toolchain and dependency versions; it can't unload; it rules out static CGO_ENABLED=0 builds. A build is a small main.go : the standard set with your extensions added, as a standalone app or a multisite host.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Your module
text: PocketOne keeps PocketBase's module path, so upstream merges stay clean. Point it at PocketOne in your go.mod : require ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase v0.41.1 replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase = github.com/pockethost/pocketone Go only honors replace in the main module, so the final binary's go.mod needs this line, not only your extension's.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Admin screens: UIExtensions
text: The dashboard loads extensions before it starts its router: Each extension is a named file system served at /_/extensions/ / . Every extension's main.js is bundled into /_/extensions.js . Add yours in the same OnServe hook: //go:embed ui var uiFiles embed.FS ui, _ := fs.Sub(uiFiles, "ui") se.UIExtensions = append(se.UIExtensions, core.UIExtension{Name: "hello", FS: ui}) ui/main.js runs in the dashboard with its UI kit ( t. ) and globals ( app.routes , app.store , app.pb ): // a new page, with a link in the header app.routes.superuserOnly("#/hello", async () = { const res = await app.pb.send("/api/hello"); return t.div({ className: "page" }, t.div({ className: "page-content" }, t.h1({}, "Hello"), t.p({}, Instance ${res.instance} )), ); }); app.store.headerLinks.push({ href: "#/hello", icon: "ri-emotion-happy-line", label: "Hello" }); // add to an existing screen: screens marked with pbEvent fire mount: with their element document.addEventListener("mount:pageBackupsSettings", (e) = { e.detail.prepend(t.p({ className: "txt-hint" }, "Hello from an extension.")); }); More hooks: app.store.settingsNavGroups adds entries to the Settings sidebar. Search pbEvent: in ui/src for every screen you can add to (Backups exposes pageBackupsSettings , backupsList , backupsSettingsForm , backupCreateModal and backupRestoreModal ). No build step: plain JS works. Bundle with Vite if you prefer. Experimental upstream: this UI extension API is undocumented and can change between PocketBase releases ( ui/README.md ). Keep main.js small, and test it after each upstream update.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Host extensions
text: A multisite host is one process serving many instances. A host extension works on that process, for every instance. Like app extensions, host extensions work together through contracts, on the host's own scope: What runs the instances (one or several, in preference order) runtime/v1 pocker, docker Which instances exist (the instance record) instance.source/v1 instances.yaml (default), mothership Admit requests (firewall, rate limits) gate/v1 firewall TLS for the host's listener tls/v1 autotls Middleware around everything http.wrap/v1 servertiming A host extension is a multisite.Extension : Name() and RegisterHost(h) , which provides its contracts on h.Scope and provides nothing when it isn't configured (no section). Pass it in multisite.Options.Extensions (in preference order), or multisite.Link it from an init so linking its package is enough. The host seals its scope once, with providers: choices for host contracts, and logs who provides what: h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Choices: providers, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{ servertiming.New(), // http.wrap/v1, outermost autotls.New(), // tls/v1 from the autotls section &pocker.Provider{}, // runtime/v1 &docker.Provider{}, // runtime/v1 too, when there's a docker section }}) multisite: runtime/v1 ← pocker, docker multisite: tls/v1 ← autotls Background work goes on h.Background , and an extension with Close(ctx) error is closed once every app has stopped. Some contracts are provided by the host for its instances (host-provided contracts), because the instance can't answer them itself: docker runs stock PocketBase images, so the host answers remote/v1 for them. The host serves them in h.InstanceRoutes , which run after the peer check, the blocked answer and the gates (firewall, rate limits) and before the runtime, with the resolved instance in multisite.InstanceOf(r) : remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(h.Scope, myRemote) h.InstanceRoutes = append(h.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler { return remotev1.W.HostHandler(h.Scope, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next) }) runtime-only hooks are pocker's Starter , SetupApp , OnStart , OnEvent and Manager (POCKER.md). App extensions that only need settings shared by every instance (mailrelay, s3-fallback, pitr) read their own pocketone.yaml section on first use and stay app extensions: they work on any host and on a single app.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Rules on a multisite host
text: On a multisite host, instances can belong to people who don't trust each other, and your Go code runs with the host's full power, outside the JS sandbox: Act only for the app you were called for. Keep per-app state in app.Store() , and use extkit.AppID(app) for anything shared that must differ per instance (a bucket prefix, a rate-limit key); never build a path from request input. Instance data needs instance auth. Protect routes that read or change it with PocketBase's auth middlewares ( apis.RequireSuperuserAuth() , record auth). Exposing something to JS is a sandbox decision. Expose a function to an instance's JS only if it's safe for a hostile tenant to call. See How is this safe?. Outbound calls follow the egress policy. Go's default HTTP client already refuses private addresses. If your extension must reach a private service, give it its own http.Client and transport, and never let instance input pick the address.

title: Create your own extension
heading: Contributing an extension
text: Extensions are welcome, from us and from you. Open a pull request that adds ext/ / .

title: Create your own extension
heading: Change PocketBase's core as little as possible
text: PocketOne stays close to upstream so every PocketBase release merges cleanly. If your extension needs something the core doesn't offer yet: Add the smallest hook that makes it possible: an extension point or an override, not your extension's logic. A nil-checked function field, a list callers can append to, or an event, with upstream behavior unchanged when nothing is registered. Make it generic. Name it for what it allows ("storage backend for an app"), not for your extension. Assume someone else's extension will use it too, and that we'll offer it to upstream PocketBase. Mark every changed line in PocketBase's own files with // PocketOne: and a few words on why, so the next upstream merge knows what to keep. Keep it separate: the core change goes in its own commit, with a test, ahead of the extension. Prefer what exists: jsvm OnInit , OnServe , the record and request hooks, BaseAppConfig.DBConnect , UIExtensions . Many extensions need no core change at all.

title: Create your own extension
heading: What an extension folder contains
text: ext/ / go.mod module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/ README.md the extension's docs, and its page on pocketone.dev (below) .go the extension _test.go conformance_test.go the shared extension test (below) example/main.go a minimal program that builds cleanly and shows the feature ui/ optional: admin screens (embedded main.js) example/main.go is required. Keep it as small as possible: just enough to build a binary that shows the feature working, with no extra harness. go build ./example and go vet ./... must pass with no warnings. ext/standard/example and ext/sandbox/example are the size to aim for. Examples come with two logins: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com (verified, in users ), both with password password . Every example/main.go calls devusers.Register(app) right after the app is created (on a multisite host, devusers.Ensure(app) in the host's per-instance setup), from ext/devusers . A fresh data dir is then ready to log in to, with no installer page and no CLI step. Never register it in a production build. conformance_test.go is required. It runs the shared extension test from ext/extkit/conformance once: func TestConformance(t testing.T) { conformance.Run(t, func() extkit.Extension { return myextension.New(myextension.Config{}) }) } It checks that the extension registers, migrates, serves and shuts down on a fresh app with no goroutines left behind; that its only routes are contracts' ( /api/_c/ / ); that PocketBase's own collections are unchanged and every collection it adds is named _ or _ _… ; and that one extension value serves several apps at once (as on a multisite host) without registering on one app touching another's hooks. An extension that requires another ( Contracts().Requires ) lists it in conformance.Options{Deps: ...} . An extension that adds MCP tools ( ext/mcp ) also passes conformance.Options{Setup: ...} that registers MCP on the test apps; the test then checks each tool is named _ _ , is described, and has an object input schema ( pb_ is reserved). Run it with go test -race . It's the minimum every extension passes; your own tests cover the feature. The README starts with front matter : who owns the extension and its version (see Ownership). owners: ["@your-github-handle"] version: 0.1.0 The README has five required sections , in this order. It is also your extension's page on pocketone.dev. ## Install : how to get it (built into pocketone , or the lines to add to a Go build). ## Configure : the pocketone.yaml section, flags and settings screens. The site adds a table of your section's keys, generated from your extkit.NewSection defaults; describe each key with a doc:"…" struct tag. ## Use : day to day: the admin screens and what to click, the commands. ## Integrations : the extensions yours works with and how (multisite hosting goes here, not in the sections above), and how other extensions can build on yours (hooks, filesystem kinds, per-instance settings, Go and REST APIs). ## Example : the code that uses it. A sentence on what your example/main.go runs, then the whole file in a differ. Without an example (an extension built into pocketone ), say where to see it used. Write the first three for someone running one PocketOne app, not for a Go developer. Anything else (how it works, limits) goes in sections after these, and extra guides can sit next to the README as other .md files. Extensions here are MIT. The README ends with ## License and the single line MIT . An extension under another license lives in its author's own repository, not here. Add your extension to site/extensions.json and run cd site/sync && go run . to build its page. ext/pitr/README.md is the example to follow. CI enforces all of this. .github/workflows/extensions.yml fails when an extension README is missing its owners and version, one of the five sections or its MIT ## License , or its Example doesn't match example/main.go , or when a module that implements extkit.Extension has no conformance test, then builds, vets and runs go test -race on every module the change affects: the modules it touches, every module that reaches one of them through a replace , or all of them for a core change. Run the same checks locally from the repository root: go run ./.github/extensions check go run ./.github/extensions affected origin/main HEAD Tests that need an external tool (MinIO, Docker) skip themselves when it isn't installed, so they don't block CI. Dependencies stay in your module. Heavy libraries go in your extension's go.mod , never in core's. Standalone first. Where it makes sense, an extension works on one standalone app, and adds more on a multisite host. MIT , like PocketBase and the rest of this repo. ### Ownership Every extension and every contract has owners, listed in its README's front matter (GitHub handles); an extension also has a version there. Whoever submits an extension or first creates a contract owns it, so an author who adds a contract with their extension owns both. Who approves an outside pull request: PocketBase's own code, the standard extensions, the site, docs, examples, CI a maintainer A community extension one of its owners, or a maintainer A contract one of its owners, or a maintainer A new extension or a new contract a maintainer Owners are read from the base branch, never from the pull request, so a pull request can't make its author an owner and approve itself. Nothing merges unless the checks pass. Every merge that changes an extension's code raises its version, and its Go module tag ( ext/ /vX.Y.Z ) follows that version. A planned extension (a README and no code yet) stays at 0.0.0 . go run ./.github/extensions approvers origin/main HEAD # who may approve each area a change touches go run ./.github/extensions versions origin/main HEAD # every extension whose code changed raised its version ## Planned extensions Our own extensions live in this repo under ext/ , each as its own Go module ( github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/ ).
